AIM :

to be able to successfully create your own flavours of kombucha, by understanding the base process

APPARATUS REQUIRED :

fermenting vessel (non reactive; glass or ceramic preferred),  boiling vessel, pressure safe bottle, freezer safe container for chilling water

REAGENTS REQUIRED :

kombucha starter/ store bought plain kombucha, tea leaves/powder (back or green, unflavoured), water,  sugar, fruits or flavouring agents

THEORY

What is kombucha ?

Kombucha is essentially fermented tea, commercially sold usually flavoured. Another way I like to describe it is 'sparkling tea', much more refined, much more appealing, but a misnomer, often used in marketing since it's a lot less intimidating to the average Joe than as compared to labelling the product as fermented tea.
The word 'ferment' invokes different ideas in the minds of different people, and to avoid the chance of a potential miscommunication, and hence a lost sale to a potential returning customers, big kombucha often resorts to calling kombucha sparkling tea to give it a sense of being something 'premium'.
Now this isn't entirely wrong, it's more of a 'all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares' sort of situation, where all fermented tea is sparkling, but not all sparkling tea is fermented. To understand why calling kombucha sparkling tea is both right and wrong, it helps understand how kombucha is made.
The end product varies completely based on many variables in the process, but in general with home brewed plain kombucha you'll end up with something effervescent, tangy and sweet, sometimes it may be a bit of a strong flavour almost akin vinegar, but that's part of the fun in making your own kombucha, the end product is highly customisable to your liking. For some the taste might be utterly repulsive, but in general it's something that grows on you with time. And if made right, it can be something you'd find quite delightful.
Commercial kombucha is often times more palatable due to the use of green tea leaves, which gives you a more mild F1, this along with the use of other commercial procedures, e.g. forced carbonation, pasteurisation, etc. which are not so viable in a home setting also contribute to the taste of a commercial brew.
If you're wondering if you can replicate the taste/experience of a commercial brew at home, the answer would be 'it depends'. The afore mentioned variables in brewing are ambient temperature, blends of tea used, time, sugar used and your initial seeding culture. Even if you followed the same recipe, many steps and the final product's taste depends on factors completely dependent on your environment, the bacteria and yeasts in your starter culture, the recipe you followed, the ingredients you used, so on and so forth, e.g. the colder your surrounding the slower your fermentation and hence the longer the process takes. 

How is kombucha made ?

You first brew a base of tea/teas, this depends on what you want, commercially a blend of green black tea leaves is used (usually 50/50),this give a more mild F1 which can be flavoured more effectively than a stronger F1, it also makes it more palatable plain to first time consumers. You then add the starter culture (as you would to turn milk to yogurt), which is a collective of bacteria and yeasts, from henceforth I will be referring to as SCOBY (symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast), which help ferment the base sweet tea into kombucha, this initial fermentation is what will is in this guide called F1 (1st fermentation).



Once the kombucha reaches ones preferred levels of tartness, one must then bottle it in a pressure safe bottle. This process is what will be referred to as F2 (2nd fermentation) from now on, this is where the kombucha gets carbonated as the carbon dioxide released as a by-product gets forced into the kombucha because it's sealed in, having nowhere else to do. Everything said so far are a massive oversimplification of the actual process, but is useful to convey the process to the uninitiated without making it seem overcomplicated and or intimidating.
It is essential to remember that your kombucha is alive, the bacteria and yeasts in your brew might not necessarily be in the exact same composition in another person' brew, think of it like a vibrant community. All around the world you see different cultures and traditions and this along with the people is what makes the community, it's the same with your brew, no two batches of kombucha are exactly the same. There is an exception to be made in the case of commercial breweries, who are held to a certain standard of consistency and often employ many unorthodox methods to meet consumer expectations. This philosophy gives you a new found sense of respect and appreciation to the whole art of fermentation involved in making kombucha.
